maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT RESPECTING OFFSHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT RESPECTING OFFSHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I announced in the house that the government would soon be able to make an important statement with respect to offshore mineral rights.
The question has been a matter of controversy for some time. Last November the Supreme Court of Canada provided an authoritative clarification of the legal position with respect to the areas off the west coast and lying outside the harbours, bays, estuaries and other similar waters which were regarded as inland waters at the time the province entered confederation. In brief, the court opinion was that the federal government is entitled to proprietary and other rights in these new areas offshore from the historic boundaries of British Columbia, which were defined generally as the ordinary low-water mark. The court thus confirmed the view previously reached by the law officers of the crown that all rights held or acquired by Canada in submerged lands lying outside the boundaries of any province accrue to Canada as a whole.

The reference to the Supreme Court was designed to determine in the most authoritative way where the jurisdiction rests. My predecessor, Mr. Pearson, indicated at the federal-provincial conference of July 1965, and I repeated in the house on September 19, that we intend to proceed now by negotiation. I

am announcing today certain steps the government is taking and certain proposals we are making to the provinces which we believe to be both important and equitable.
In the light of the Supreme Court's unanimous finding in favour of the crown in right of Canada, on the basis of principles that would appear to be substantially applicable to the east coast as well as to the west coast, the main problem becomes one of delineating the areas concerned to meet the practical requirements of mineral resource administration. That is, it is necessary to establish lines for the purpose of differentiating between submerged lands to be administered by the federal government and lands to be administered by the provincial governments.
There are certain difficulties in using for this purpose the boundaries described by the court, since it is difficult to ascertain what would have been considered as a bay or harbour for the purposes of international or domestic law at the time most of the provinces entered confederation, and since the lines of low tide are shifting and uncertain and our seacoasts are characterized by deep indentations, straits, innumerable islands, and inlets of various configurations.

After exploring a number of alternatives, it has been found that the geodetic grid system provides the best basis for delineation of areas of offshore administration. This method is already utilized for the issuance of exploration permits. The geodetic grid system is the reference system of lines of longitude and latitude used to identify the precise positions of points on the earth's surface. Using this system we have drawn so-called mineral resource administration lines, always well within the area of federal jurisdiction on the basis of the principles laid down in the Supreme Court opinion, with the intention that the federal government will administer all offshore mineral rights seaward from these lines. It should be noted that the mineral resource administration lines are not to be confused with the base lines from which Canada's territorial sea and fishing zones are measured in keeping with international law.
We are taking into account the undertaking of equitable arrangements made by Mr. Pearson. We are offering to work out in conjunction with each of the coastal provinces a
December 2, 1968

method whereby they would in effect administer any offshore mineral rights under federal jurisdiction on the landward side of the mineral resource administration lines. In addition the federal government is prepared to concede to the coastal provinces all revenues derived from the mineral resources of the submerged lands within these lines.
The proposed administrative lines enclose several offshore areas which are linked closely with adjacent provincial lands. Off the west coast these include the sea bottom between Vancouver island and the mainland, as well as appreciable areas in close proximity to the mainland and offlying islands. Off the east coast they include large areas of the sea bottom in the bay of Fundy, Northumberland strait and the passage Jacques-Cartier. These areas will also include historic bays and waters adjacent to numerous offlying islands thus making substantial territories available for administration by each of the coastal provinces.

In view of the many aspects of national significance involved, the government regards it as essential to retain the administration and management of mineral resources seaward from the mineral resource administration lines. With respect to the revenues, however, Mr. Speaker, the government wishes to seek a fair and reasonable basis whereby the provincial governments would share in the revenues that may be derived from these national resources which lie off the coasts of the provinces. It would be the intention to place the revenues accruing from these resources in a single national pool from which half the revenues would be made available to the provinces concerned. This would be purely a financial arrangement and would not imply involvement by the provinces in the jurisdiction and administration of mineral resources in those areas beyond mineral resource administration lines.
I am issuing today maps showing the locations of the mineral resource administration lines off both the east and west coasts. Similar lines will also be drawn in the regions of Hudson Strait, Hudson Bay, and James Bay, where it will also be necessary to define a boundary between the submerged lands adjacent to the provinces and those adjacent to the Northwest Territories and Arctic Islands. Acceptance of the mineral resource administration lines is the necessary first step in resolving the offshore situation. We can then work together with the provinces in finding a
Dominion-Provincial Relations satisfactory basis upon which the provincial share of revenues would be divided.

The question of the basis upon which the provincial share of revenues would be divided is one on which the federal government is open to suggestions. We would be agreeable to any proposal that the provincial governments themselves feel is acceptable. It may be that in discussions among themselves the provinces have already touched upon a basis or method which can be utilized in this connection. We would be prepared to hold the provincial share of revenues in escrow for a reasonable time until a satisfactory formula has been decided upon. If it would help in reaching an acceptable solution within a reasonable period, we would be willing to make constructive suggestions. I have written on Friday to the premiers on this subject, and I hope they will respond favourably to the federal offer within a relatively short time. Then we can proceed to work out details.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
It is essential to reach a settlement of the offshore situation with all possible dispatch. The continental shelf areas adjacent to Canada comprise a vast new territory estimated to be almost 40 per cent as large as the total land area of Canada. Several regions favourable for the development of mineral resources are probably present, particularly as concerns oil and gas.
It is clearly in the interest of all levels of government that conditions are such as to facilitate the rapid development of Canada's offshore minerals. For our part we wish to do everything possible to avoid jurisdictional disputes that would hinder or delay the development of these natural resources. This is the spirit in which we are offering to work out these arrangements with the provinces.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT RESPECTING OFFSHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the Prime Minister with great interest. This is indeed an important subject. It has been estimated that there are 250 years supply of oil alone beneath the sea, based on present yearly consumption, and that the continental shelf contains as much mineral wealth per square mile as dry land. So it is indeed a very important matter with which the Prime Minister has dealt today.
First I want to say quite clearly that it is not possible at this stage to indicate that the proposals made by the Prime Minister are in fact equitable, or to examine clearly the extent to which there will be fair sharing between the provincial governments and the federal government under the terms of the proposals he has made. That has to be considered later. However, I would make several other comments.
In his statement the Prime Minister said we intend to proceed now by negotiation. As I listened to him delineate very clearly what the federal government intended to do and what the provincial governments would be allowed to do, it struck me at first blush that there was remarkably little negotiation involved. It may well be that as the matter proceeds further negotiation will indeed be permitted, but if the Prime Minister is saying on behalf of the federal government "This is the way we intend to do it", and the provinces will be entitled only to such resources as lie within the area delineated in his statement, then I say this falls far short of the true kind of negotiation which we should expect.
There are still one or two questions which have to be answered. Certainly this is not the forum in which to go into details, but to what extent is the judgment applicable on a national scale? The Prime Minister indicates that it does have national application, but as one examines the answers given by the Supreme Court of Canada to the questions, one discovers those were specific answers to specific questions related to the province of British Columbia alone. While it may be true that these proceeded on certain principles, I think it is a well known legal maxim that where there is a specific question, and a specific reference, the answers are applicable only to that reference.
This is a question which must yet be determined. In spite of the fact that the Prime Minister has indicated that the law officers of the crown, in the right of the federal government, have taken a certain view, this may not necessarily be the view which the provincial governments will take.


The second question is, to what extent is the federal government free to negotiate, to give away or withhold as it sees fit, resources which its legal advisers have told it belong to all the people of Canada, resources which, pursuant to the constitutional decisions, to the British North American Act and other constitutional statutes, belong to all the people of Canada? To what extent would it be possible for the federal government to make a binding disposition of such resources without such a decision being subject to challenge? I cannot take any position at this time, but I think this is a very important question which must still be decided. Certainly if the Prime Minister's statement is a basis for discussion and negotiation between the federal government and the provinces that is fine; but I suggest through you, Mr. Speaker, to the members of this house that the only type of decision which in fact can be fair and probably binding in law as well as in equity is one arrived at after full discussion between the provincial and federal governments. Until that time comes we will have to look at this issue very, very carefully.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT RESPECTING OFFSHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Prime Minister for his courtesy in sending us in advance a copy of this important statement. I confess that when an opposition spokesman receives a statement an hour in advance, he spends that time in trying to find things that are wrong with the statement. I must also confess that in the hour I had I found little that one can really complain about so far as this statement is concerned.
The importance of this subject is impressed upon us by the remarks the Prime Minister made and by the statistics just given by the hon. member for Peace River. We also realize that there is a very real issue at stake, namely to whom shall go the revenues from the huge oil and mineral resources that probably are to be found under the waters adjoining this country.
It seems to me that the essence of the Prime Minister's statement is very simple; that is, the jurisdiction is clearly federal, but common sense calls for some sort of a share the wealth program. We see this statement as seeking to implement those two principles, and to that extent it would seem to us to merit the approval of the house.
I did look in this statement for some reference to the international aspect of this whole question of mineral resources under the sea. It would seem that this has become a subject of concern at the United Nations. I looked for
December 2, 1968

something in the statement, but it was not there. Perhaps we will get that on another occasion. I welcome the fact that the Prime Minister has taken the position that the matter is federal and, therefore, that certain decisions have to be declared a starting point but that the federal government is prepared to negotiate with the provinces from that point on. I hope there will be an early effort, on the part of both the federal and provincial governments, to settle this very important question.
We are grateful to the Prime Minister for having made this statement without further delay. It is a very important issue.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS STATEMENT RESPECTING OFFSHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all we wish to thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for his statement on off-shore mineral rights.
I should like to make a brief remark on one specific point, namely the sharing of revenues derived from the exploitation of mineral resources means or suggests the sharing of responsibilities. The federal government having indicated that consultations would be held with the provinces with regard to the basis for the distribution of half the revenues derived from mineral resources. I feel that the provinces will also wish to participate in the administration and operation. Now, if the statement of the right hon. Prime Minister is studied carefully, it does not seem sure that the provinces can participate directly in the operation or administration if the federal government takes over those rights and it may not necessarily be to blame. I feel that it is a matter of jurisdiction and once again we go back to the very basis of our constitution which must delineate clearly the responsibilities of the federal and provincial governments.
Mr. Speaker, if this case is treated the way Labrador was, I fear that no solution will be reached. The privy council reached a decision in 1927 concerning the ownership of Labrador which led to a now historical bone of contention. It was to decide to whom Labrador belonged-to Quebec, to Newfoundland or to the federal government-and the privy council settled the matter in 1927. A few months ago the right hon. Prime Minister replied to me saying that nothing had changed and I think that the federal government does certain things when they serve its purpose, but it remains mute when that is more suitable. I should therefore like to take this opportunity to speak to the extremely timely statement of the Prime Minister and urge him to reconsid-
Questions
er his decision concerning the ownership of Labrador, because I feel it is somewhat related to the matter now under discussion, that is off-shore mineral rights.
I therefore feel that it would be both in the interest of the federal government and the provinces to meet and define clearly the jurisdiction of the governments, on the federal and provincial level, because, in the final analysis, it concerns the very essence of the B.N.A. Act.

Mr. Speaker, I direct a question to the Prime Minister in connection with the statement he read to the house today. I do not
December 2, 1968

know whether I missed the answer to the question I am about to ask. If I did, it is only because I did not hear that portion of the statement.
The situation in provinces other than British Columbia, that is the provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Quebec, Ontario and the maritime provinces, is quite different basically and juridically, and I am wondering why the request for the viewpoint of the Supreme Court of Canada regarding the ownership of offshore minerals in these provinces was not submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada before the Prime Minister decided on setting out in detail the attitude to be taken by the government of Canada.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS APPLICATION OF SUPREME COURT DECISION TO PROVINCES OTHER THAN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the right hon. gentleman is asking why it had not been done before, I can only say that it was another government that decided to submit this reference in this particular way. With regard to why it is not being done now before making the statement, I think the best answer is that this type of reference is a lengthy procedure. It might take months of litigation and waiting for the rendering of a decision. It is in order to gain time that the government has proceeded in this fashion.
I agree with the right hon. gentleman that there are some distinctions in law to be drawn between the various situations. But we feel the underlying principles are much the same and we prefer to go ahead now with a negotiated settlement, if it is possible, rather than embark upon possibly years of litigation; because it is extremely urgent that all Canadians should reach some kind of agreement as soon as possible in order that the exploitation of these resources be begun as quickly as possible.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS APPLICATION OF SUPREME COURT DECISION TO PROVINCES OTHER THAN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
The question of time is always important, Mr. Speaker, but there is a matter of great principle here. I am wondering whether the Prime Minister has given consideration to asking the Supreme Court of Canada to permit an early submission to them for their opinion. It would not take very long. It did not take very long in regard to the submission respecting British Columbia. I am sure the Supreme Court of Canada, in view of the importance of this matter, would give the Prime Minister the assurance that at the earliest possible date an opinion would be given. Otherwise these provinces which have a different juridical position than British Columbia find themselves in an impossible position.

speechtext: I think the answer to the hon. member's problem, Mr. Speaker, may be that there was a reference to mining rights which belong to the provinces, and which under the arrangement we propose would continue to belong to the provinces. speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, there has been no special communication of that nature with the provinces. Once again we took the position that, certainly in the case of the province of British Columbia, we were drawing lines well within the territory which was allocated to the federal government, and therefore we were leaning in favour of the provincial side. We felt we were giving more to the provinces than the court obliged us to do in this particular case. We followed the same principles, as I just indicated in answering a previous question, in drawing the resource administration lines in the case of other provinces, keeping always well on the outside of what might be interpreted to be historically provincial seas or waters. It is for this reason we are trying to avoid litigation, by being as generous as possible even with territorial seas which normally might be suspected, under international law, to be federal. We hope, by avoiding litigation, to advance this whole question much more quickly for the benefit of all the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since the creation of the Department of Industry in 1963 the department has introduced numerous programs to assist Canadian industry in increasing its productivity and expanding its output. These programs have made industry more competitive and have contributed appreciably to the success of the manufactured products sector of Canadian exports. Indeed, during the past five years Canada's exports of manufactured products have increased fourfold and now account for about 34 per cent of total exports.
It is interesting to observe the growth of the manufactured products sector of Canadian exports. In 1958, it amounted to 13.2 per cent; in 1963, to 15.4 per cent, in 1967, to 31.2 per cent and this year to about 34 per cent. As a result, exports of processed manufactured products now make up nearly three-quarters of total Canadian exports. Furthermore, some of the greatest gains in expanded production and increased exports have been in the more sophisticated product lines.
A few moments ago I was reading a paper on the subject of productivity. Canadian manufacturing compares favourably, the paper said, with that of most countries, but productivity in the United States is still more than 30 per cent higher than in Canada. However, Canada has been successful in

reducing this productivity gap. While productivity in United States manufacturing has increased by some 80 per cent over the postwar period, manufacturing productivity in-Canada has more than doubled. The narrowing of the gap was continued during the last decade during which Canada reported a 43 per cent increase compared with 36 per cent in the United States. Apparently the gap is still about 30 per cent for the whole industrial sector. Hon. members will no doubt understand the importance of reducing this gap as much and as fast as possible, since this is a major determinant in international competitiveness and consequently a major factor in the success of Canadian exports.
Canada has improved its production and export performance, as I have indicated, in a number of product areas such as electronic equipment, aircraft and aircraft components, and this improvement is directly attributable to special arrangements and programs in which the Department of Industry has played a leading role.
May I now tell you a few things, Mr. Chairman, about the automotive industry program. Substantial progress has been made toward the attainment of the objectives of the 1965 program. By 1968 the production of passenger vehicles had increased by 29 per cent and commercial vehicles by more than 129 per cent, over the levels for 1964, the year immediately preceding implementation of the program.
The surge in trade has been even more spectacular. In 1964 Canada exported automotive products valued at $136 million. By the model of 1968 the export of such products amounted to a value exceeding $2 billion.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Of course imports have also risen but the trade imbalance in automotive products, which had been growing rapidly in previous years, was reduced for the first time in 1966, and it will be further diminished in 1968. The projection for 1968 indicates that the imbalance may be about $364 million world wide, $350 million of that with the United States. When one compares that figure with the figure of $683 million for 1966 and $547 million for 1965, one easily realizes the tremendous progress which has been made.
Average levels of employment in the automotive industries have also increased during the life of the program, from a monthly average of 68,000 in 1964 to about 80,000 people in 1968.
December 2, 1968

An appreciable amount of rationalization of production has taken place both in the assembly of vehicles and in the manufacture of parts. Although total production of motor cars has increased appreciably, the number of car makes, body styles and models assembled in Canada has been reduced considerably. This was a condition of the success of the over-all operation.
Productivity has also improved in the automotive industries. Traditionally productivity in the Canadian automotive industries has been well below that of the United States. The trend to a greater variety of models and styles intensified this problem for Canadian producers, but under the new program, with a bigger output of fewer models, it has been possible to achieve greater specialization and, consequently, greater productivity. During the period 1961 to 1963 the average annual increase in productivity was 5 per cent with respect to vehicles assembled in Canada. From 1965 to 1967 this annual increase reached 8 per cent, and so it is estimated that the productivity gap between Canada and the United States in the automotive field has now been reduced to about 20 per cent. This is obviously still too high, and efforts will be made by all concerned to reduce it further.
The success of the over-all operation was not entirely painless. In order to take advantage of these production and trade opportunities many parts manufacturers have found it necessary to undertake major re-equipment and expansion programs. Smaller manufacturers in Canada have always formed an important part of the automotive industry. These firms wished to play a role under the automotive program, which was designed in several specific ways to take their interests into account. For them the Department of Industry introduced the automotive adjustment assistance program to ensure that they would be able to obtain adequate financing on reasonable terms in order to modernize and reequip their plants. This program provides for loans to automotive parts manufacturers and suppliers of materials, accessories and tooling used in the automotive industry. The repayment period of a loan made under this program is related to the borrower's capacity to repay and the circumstances of the loan, and may extend over a period of up to 20 years.
Since the initiation of the program 68 loans valued at $55 million have been made to assist Canadian automotive producers to expand their operations and make them more efficient, and 17 other cases are presently under investigation.
Supply-Industry
Also, in order to reduce the costs of Canadian automotive parts makers and thus improve their ability to compete for North American markets, a program has been initiated by the department to remit duties on imported production machinery and equipment which are not available from Canadian producers within the time needed to meet production schedules. In order to keep hon. members informed of the growth of this program, I might indicate that my information to April 29, 1968, shows that 170 applications have been received and remissions of $2.9 million have been granted. My latest figures with respect to the amount of remissions show $3.24 million in remissions on machinery imported into Canada. This is so much expense that the producers did not have to meet.
Many Canadian parts manufacturers are now supplying not only the domestic markets but are shipping substantial quantities of components to export markets.
I know, Mr. Chairman, that you are quite aware of the importance of the Kennedy round of tariff negotiations, and you may like to know that the Department of Industry has been involved in developing programs in order to make it possible for Canadian manufacturers to take advantage of all the possibilities afforded by the Kennedy round.
The first program I would like to mention is the general adjustment assistance program, which was announced in March, 1968, very recently, relatively speaking. In circumstances of freer world trade it was essential that Canada's secondary industry should develop greater competitive strength. This situation directed that the major objectives of industrial adjustment policy should be, (a) to derive as much benefit as possible from widening markets and increasing scope for greater specialization and longer production runs, and (b) to assist firms adversely affected to adapt effectively to more competitive conditions. These are the purposes of the general adjustment assistance program.
The first feature of the program is the offer, by the Department of Industry, of insurance on the major share of the risk of loss on adjustment assistance loans made by private lenders. The second feature is the offer of direct loans to firms that have been seriously injured, or threatened with serious injury, as a result of reductions in the Canadian tariff, and which are unable to borrow the funds they require from the private sector under the insured loan program. The

December 2, 1968
Supp ly-Industry
third feature of the program is the offer of technical and professional advice to firms. The department will share the cost of such consulting services with the firm to the extent considered appropriate in each case, but the department's share will not exceed 50 per cent.
These are the three features of the general adjustment assistance program. Again, one is insurance of loans made by the private sector, the second is direct loans, and the third is technical assistance.
To date 377 inquiries have been received, 90 per cent of which have been for insurance of private loans and 10 per cent for direct loans. A total of 80 cases are under direct study, two have been approved and one has been rejected.
It is estimated that in the next five years insured loans totalling half a billion dollars and direct loans totalling $45 million will be made under this program. Requirements for consulting grants are expected to amount to $5 million in the same period. For 1968-69 we are asking spending authority for direct loans and consulting grants in the amount of $10 million-that is vote L75-and $1 million under vote 3.

I would now like to say a word about another program of the Department of Industry, arising from the Kennedy Round, the machinery program. It is an extension of what I said earlier about the machinery program within the framework of the Can-ada-U.S. automotive agreement.
This program, which is defined by tariff item 42700-1 and came into force on January 1, 1968, has a twofold objective. Its first purpose is to promote greater efficiency by enabling the industry to get production equipment at the lowest possible prices. Secondly, it enables the Canadian machinery industry, that is machinery producers, to make the best possible use of the rate which, in the future, will apply with more certainty to the products they make.
Allow me to explain, Mr. Chairman. The main aspects of that program are twofold. First, it will set up a single tariff for imported machinery. Those duties which until now could reach 22J per cent are now set at 15 per cent for the countries enjoying the most favoured nation status and at 2J per cent for those enjoying the British preferential tariff. All those tariffs which varied
[Mr. Pepin. 1
so much previously have been reduced to a single tariff of 15 per cent.
It will be recalled that previously Canadian machinery producers had to prove that they were in a position to meet 10 per cent of local consumer needs before getting that protection. They no longer have to prove that; now, once again, they are automatically protected, and by a single tariff.
The second aspect of that program is a provision allowing for the remission of customs duties by the governor in council, upon the recommendation of the Minister of Industry, when such machinery is not made by Canadian producers and such remission is in the public interest. That is, I think, a happy compromise between the interests of the buyer-importer, that is the man who needs the machinery to produce other things, and the interests of the Canadian machinery producers.
It is impossible, in fact, to produce in Canada all the equipment needed by our industry. The needs are too varied and very often machinery producers in other countries have developed special machines and it would not be very economic for us to try to compete. Therefore, that equipment not produced in Canada enters the country duty free -because of that program and in the best interest of the buyer, the Canadian industrialist and also, I think, the Canadian public.
On the other hand, if a Canadian company produces that type of machinery, its market is reasonably well protected. I feel this is an excellent compromise between the interests of the manufacturer, who needs equipment and must pay as little as possible for it, and those of the Canadian machinery producer. That is the compromise the legislation I have mentioned has put into effect.
The program applies to approximately 60 per cent of the $700 million worth of annual imports in that field. One can see therefore that the program will cost the receiver general, in losses, roughly $45 million a year. I feel everyone will admit that this is an excellent piece of legislation.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I should also like to say a few words on the important program on productivity in the defence material or military equipment industry. That program takes in two others: the defence export development program set up in 1964, and the defence industries plant modernization program set up in 1959. You
December 2, 1968

will find those estimates under votes 5 and L75.
The defence industry production program has four objectives:
First, to reduce the purchase price of military material purchased by the Canadian Department of National Defence for the use of the Canadian army.
Second, to develop, in Canada, an industrial capacity in the field of military equipment, with a view to its benefiting from the international agreements between Canada and its allies in the sharing of military equipment production contracts. As you know, there are agreements between Canada and the States, Canada and England and others the purpose of which is to enable the producers in each one of those countries to benefit from the defence contracts in the other countries.
Those then are the two first aims but it seems that the others are at least as important.
Third, to benefit from the advantages of highly advanced modem technology and administrative techniques, usually inherent in military research and production which are often in the very forefront of the technological and business management development. The program aims directly to allow Canadian industrial sectors to benefit from this progress.
Fourth, to increase progressively civil applications that are directly related to military production and sometimes depend upon it. I believe all members know to what extent progress in the industrial civil field is closely related to the one in the militry equipment field. One very seldom sees an ultra-modern product, ahead of its time in the industrial field, that has not been influenced by defence contracts distributed in Canada or in other countries; this is due to the close relations existing nowadays between the military and civil areas of industrial development. We may not like it, we may deplore it, but it is a fact, if not unavoidable, at least undeniable.
Under such a program, Mr. Chairman, government aid is granted to that industry to enable it to obtain, before any preliminary technical work, the necessary equipment for the production of new products designed in Canada for the world markets.

Among the projects that have received assistance are communications and aircraft navigation systems, gas turbine engines for
Supply-Industry
aircraft, flight safety and simulation equipment, information display facilities, and so on. Since its inception 165 projects have been supported under this program. Expenditures today amount to $148 million. Of the projects supported, some 120 costing $99 million have been completed and are achieving sales. The value of sales resulting from these is expected to reach $2.4 billion during the sales life of the products. There obviously have been a few failures, but there have been a number of success stories in these cases of assistance given by the federal government for the development of the defence industry.
I would have liked to say more about industrial research and development, but the time is getting short. In this field the department has three major programs.
The first is the industrial research institutes program. In December, 1966, the department introduced a plan to assist Canadian universities in establishing and administering industrial research institutes. The basic aim is to draw on university staff and facilities to help alleviate the shortage of scientific and technical resources available to industry as a whole and to provide scientific services to smaller firms which cannot afford to maintain and staff their own research facilities. Grants to four Canadian universities totalling about $475,000 had been approved under the program by the end of the year. For this year we are asking $240,000.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The next program is more important at least in financial terms. It is called the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act. The initials are IRDIA. That is a name I would not give to my daughter but it describes well, the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act. This act, dated June 1967, has been providing general incentives to industry for the expansion of scientific research and development in Canada. Under section 70 of the federal Income Tax Act an allowance can be made for deduction of all expenditures of a current and capital nature made for scientific research. Over and above that, under IRDIA, Canadian Corporations are also entitled to apply to the department for a cash grant or for a credit against federal income tax liabilities amounting to 25 per cent of all their capital expenditures for scientific research and development in Canada, and 25 per cent of the increase in their current expenditures in Canada for scientific research and development over the average

December 2, 1968
Supply-[DOT]Industry
of such expenditures in the preceding five years.
Corporations must undertake to exploit the results of their research and development work in Canada and must be free to market products resulting from their research and development to all countries in the world. As of today, December 2, 728 applications for grants totalling $44,500,000 have been received. A total of 318 applications to the value of $8 million have been approved, and we have $31.3 million in the vote for 1968-69.
The last of these programs for industrial research is PAIT, program for the advancement of industrial technology. Under this program the department underwrites the development of new or improved products or processes which involve a significant advance in technology and which offer good prospects for commercial exploitation. The department pays 50 per cent of the development costs. If the project is successful there is an obligation for repayment, but if it is a failure no such obligation exists.
Forty new development projects estimated to cost $8 million were approved in 1968, bringing the total number of projects supported under the program since its inauguration to 160 valued at $44 million.
One interesting detail is that several companies which have successfully completed projects have begun to repay the department's contribution. Another interesting detail is that 22 of these projects were successfully completed. Their cost was $1,400,000 and the sales potential is $95 million in five years. So, for an investment of $1,400,000 we will have a sales potential for these Canadian goods of $95 million. The benefit ratio is rather extraordinary. I cannot say they are all like that, but a good number of them have been.

I should like to conclude my remarks by taking a minute or two to talk about industrial design. The improvement of industrial design, or industrial aesthetics, if you prefer, is one of the most important ways there are to make Canadian products more competitive.
To this end, the department has set up several programs of assistance to industry and of consumer information. A sum of $678,430 will be allocated to those programs in 1968-69. I shall mention only some of those programs.
There is the "Canada-Design 67". I should perhaps say first of all that the word "design" is accepted, even in French. This program

was undertaken in 1965 in order to promote the manufacturing of Canadian products which could be used for centennial projects. This allowed reference lists on the aesthetic merits of the various products to be drawn up for the use of those who planned the centennial projects.
"Canada-Design 67" catalogues were distributed to many architects, contractors and buyers, as well as to retail salesmen and businessmen, both in Canada and abroad.
In order to stimulate further the sale of these products, a series of Design 67 exhibitions were organized in various centres in Canada and they attracted more than 100,000 visitors. The products which attracted the most attention were also widely publicized in Canadian and foreign newspapers.
During the whole of Expo 67 the Department made a study of products especially conceived for our universal exhibition in order to select those which could best lend themselves to commercial production. This project goes under the name "Design Expo 67." 150 products were selected as worthy of commercial promotion, and catalogues were prepared containing photographs, the name of the manufacturer, prices and other information concerning these products.
The department organized two design competitions, the costs being shared with industrialist associations. The object was to recognize the achievements of Canadian designers by offering prizes to the best works, and publicity to their authors. The Design Canada structural steel competition, designed to reward the authors of remarkable achievements in an original application of structural steel to the construction of buildings and bridges, attracted 62 competitors.
There was another competition for concrete works. I have a. long list, Mr. Chairman, but I will spare the details to the house.
The year 1967 has seen the outcome of an important project: the opening of a new Design Canada Centre at Place Bonaventure, in Montreal. Here again, the purpose is to improve aesthetic qualities of products made in Quebec in particular, and in Canada in general. Furthermore, the Toronto Design Canada Centre is stirring an ever-increasing interest among the public; 84,786 people visited it this year as against 46,614 last year. Nine specialized exhibitions have been set up there.
Before closing, I should like to mention the Design Canada service. As one can see, Mr. Chairman, I am trying to advertise a little
December 2, 1968

these various sectors of my department which have obvious merits. It is a consulting service intended for Canadian industrialists so that they may collect material on matters of design. The Design Canada service includes a reference library, books, periodicals, technical movements, and a repertory of Canadian industrial designers which includes information on the members of the profession and the specialized services in this field.
In the field of design, Mr. Speaker, I have been and I continue to be particularly interested since, in my opinion, if Canadian products do not compete with foreign products as to appearance, in this sector, that is, if they are sturdy and well-made, but inelegant and unattractive, tremendous opportunities for sales, and for exports in particular, will certainly be missed.
These are, Mr. Speaker, some comments on the activities of my department. I could say a lot more but I shall provide now my hon. colleagues with the opportunity to give me some advice.

Mr. Chairman, we appreciate the minister's introductory remarks in respect of the estimates of the Department of Industry, but I would much rather he had taken the time to tell us whether there is a Department of Industry, whether his department is industry and trade and commerce, or just exactly where we are in this program of amalgamation or unification. We in this house have not passed legislation setting up this department.

[DOT] (4:30 p.m.l

I am still confused. I understand that the Department of Industry has been dismantled and is in the process of being amalgamated with trade and commerce. We
Supply-Industry
have even gone so far as to call it the department of industry, trade and commerce in the blue book of estimates. I am confused on this issue. The minister says we are discussing the estimates of the Department of Industry. This department is being amalgamated with the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the Department of Trade and Commerce has moved from its original building on Wellington Street to the building which housed the Department of Industry. There is great confusion amongst the staff of the two departments. They do not know for whom they work. They do not know how/or where they are being fitted into the new department or program. I also hear there is a problem in fitting in some of the officials who were hired by the Department of Industry at much higher salaries than the prevailing salaries in the Department of Trade and Commerce. When you try to fit such a person into a lower pay schedule it creates a problem which I can quite easily understand.
In 1963 we on this side of the house gave the government of the day our views on setting up a department of industry. We said we thought it was folly and foolish to do so. We thought that the existing Department of Trade and Commerce could do anything the Department of Industry would endeavour to do. We were told that it would not be an expensive operation, that the government would take staff from the Department of Defence Production and the Department of Trade and Commerce and move them to the Department of Industry. However, when you look back on the whole program you see it has been nothing but a great big bill of expense. It has been a tremendous expense to the Canadian taxpayer.
The Department of Industry started in 1963-64 with a staff of 274. The next year that staff jumped to 786, an increase of 512 employees or 200 per cent. That is staff alone. With regard to money, in 1968 the estimates which this house approved totalled $117,586,000 to operate the Department of Industry. Now it is all being shattered, broken up and moved over to trade and commerce and all this money has gone down the drain. All this could have been saved by just adding to the department of trade and commerce the word "industry" and the taxpayers of this country would have been saved a great deal of money. But they have to pay the tune because the government would not listen to the advice of the Conservative opposition. Be that as it

I will be very brief in my remarks, Mr. Chairman. The minister made many very interesting observations about the Canada-U.S. Auto pact. I thank him for that. He gave us a great many statistics. I know he does not like statistics any more than I do. Nevertheless he had them prepared for him and gave them to us. They will be useful to look back on and read at our leisure. The minister also gave us all the highlights of the Canada-U.S. car pact, but I am still of the opinion I had when the pact was arrived at, namely, that the one fundamental point is that if you lose your economic birthright you lose your political birthright. By giving all these advantages to American subsidiaries in Canada we are handing them our political birthright. I think this is as true today as it was when the pact was instituted.
Another thing the minister and the government will have to sell to the Canadian public before this pact is a success is that the Canadian purchaser can buy a made in Canada automobile at the same price as his American cousin who lives in, say, Detroit. A car is made in Oakville, Canada, and shipped to Detroit, and an American can buy the same car for $200 or $300 less than a Canadian. When Canadians can purchase cars made in this country at the same price as Americans can, we will have proved to Canadian taxpayers that this program has been partially worth while and that they share the so-called benefit which the minister outlined this afternoon.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, we must not forget that at the time the pact was introduced we gave to the car manufacturers over $50 million in tariffs which we had previously collected. We gave this amount of money to the car manufacturers and allowed them to sell Canadian made cars in the United States for less money than we in Canada can buy them. When the Canadian purchaser of an automobile has the same benefit, the minister will have proven that the pact has been somewhat successful.
With the U.S.-Canada car pact came some very good things. I said at the time that there were two sides to every coin and there would be some good and some bad points to the pact. The minister has told us only about the good points this afternoon. He did not say it

was responsible for bringing into Canada parity of wages not only in this industry but in many other industries in Canada to which it has spread. There will be many more industries affected as time goes on. The minister did not tell us about the growing number of small industries that have been put out of business. He did not tell us that the large industries have been getting larger and the small ones getting smaller to the point where they had been forced out of business.
Members of the house who had in their ridings small manufacturers of car parts will tell you that these businesses have disappeared. The farther you go from the border, the more you will find they have disappeared. They have been replaced by larger industries which are in turn subsidiaries of American companies. This means there is more control by the United States of the Canadian economy. We have lost more of our political strength when we should be maintaining or regaining it. However, this was the government's decision and we just hope for the best. I might have missed some of the statistics the minister gave, but I think he dwelt more on export figures than on imports. We must remember that a great many cars and trucks have been imported into Canada, which fact offsets many of our exports.
However, Mr. Chairman, we are not here to debate the Canada-U.S. car pact but to study the estimates of the once Department of Industry. The minister says this department still exists. I propose to leave time for hon. members to deal with these estimates. Before we leave the matter of the amalgamation of departments and the setting up of new departments may I tell the committee that I know of a person who came to Ottawa to discuss a problem with the Department of Industry because he believed that department was concerned in his problem. He went to the Department of Industry and they told him it was not their problem and he should go to the Department of Trade and Commerce. He went to the Department of Trade and Commerce and was advised that it was really a problem for the Department of Industry. Finally the problem was settled by the Department of Labour. This man spent the greatest part of a day travelling between departments before he found the right one to deal with his problem. This illustrates the state of confusion that exists in these departments. I hope the situation will be ironed out before too long and that when a manufacturer comes to Ottawa with a problem he will be able to go to the Department of Industry,

Mr. Chairman, as I listened to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce extol the virtues of the Canada-United States auto pact I was reminded of the words of the former minister of industry when he proposed the plan. It seemed to me that, although this minister is a French Canadian and the former minister is an English Canadian, really the more things change in a Liberal government the more they are the same. We have had an explanation of this plan which reminded me of the famous maxim of Mr. Charles Wilson when he was secretary of defence for the United States. Mr. Wilson had been president of the General Motors Corporation. On one occasion he said, "what is good for G.M. is good for the American people". As I listened to the minister I could not help but think that the minister really had the same view, that what is good for the auto companies of Canada must be good for the Canadian people. Certainly that is not entirely true.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I remind the minister and members of the house that the purpose of the auto pact was to provide free trade, not for you, Mr. Chairman, or for me or other buyers of automobiles in Canada but for the giant automobile companies in the United States and their mouse partners in Canada. It enabled them to rationalize their production to the extent that they could exchange automobiles and automobile parts without paying the customary duty. What the minister did not tell us this afternoon was that the sweetener that the Canadian people gave these poor automobile companies like General Motors, Ford and Chrysler, who between them own billions of dollars worth of assets in the United States, Canada and other countries in the world, was $50

million in tax revenue as an inducement to enter this pact.
When the pact was first proposed the then minister told the Canadian people that one of the results of the pact would be a reduction in automobile prices in Canada to the extent that the price in Canada would approximate that paid in the United States for the same automobile. For many years we were told that automobile prices in Canada had to be substantially higher than prices in the United States because the market in Canada was much smaller, the production run for individual models was smaller, and therefore productivity was lower and automobiles cost more. The minister has already said that as a result of the pact the industry has been rationalized to a large extent and the number of models manufactured in Canadian factories has been cut sharply. There is a flow from Canada to the United States which has made productivity in both Canada and the U.S. increase.
When he introduced this pact the former minister of industry, now President of the Treasury Board, in a statement on January 15, 1965, dealing with the effect of the pact on the cost of automobiles had this to say:
Of significance for the Canadian consumer is the fact that over several years, the plan should progressively make possible increased efficiency and reduced costs. Indeed, this is one of the principal objectives of the entire program. In line with the attainment of lower costs of production, it is to be anticipated, as the program develops, that the forces of competition will gradually result in savings for Canadian consumers in the form of a narrowing differential between Canadian and United States prices for motor vehicles and components.
It was not only the opposition members of parliament who took the minister seriously, Mr. Chairman. The Vancouver Sun, a newspaper that members from British Columbia will know better than I to be a supporter of the Liberal party, published an editorial in its edition of April 14, 1965, from which I should like to place on record one or two sentences:
Among other things, Mr. Walter Gordon's forthcoming budget will have to defend the Canadian-American free trade deal in automotive products. It can be easily defended if it means that automobile prices will soon fall. If they don't, the deal is quite indefensible.
Then the Winnipeg Free Press, published in my own city, made this comment in its issue of April 17, 1965.
A much larger question now faces the Canadian government as a result of the free trade deal. It is whether this ostensibly constructive agreement will do any good for the Canadian consumer or whether it will benefit only a few rich automobile manufacturers.

These comments were made two and a half years ago, Mr. Chairman. What is the position today? The hon. member for Wellington who has just resumed his seat referred to the fact that even making allowance for the price differential between Canada and the United States and the different government taxes, both federal and provincial, cars produced in Oakville and sold in Buffalo are cheaper than the same models sold in Toronto. Therefore we must ask ourselves how this is possible. Either the Ford Motor Company is selling in Buffalo cars produced at Oakville at a loss

 and I do not think that even the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce believes that-or the price the company charges in Canada for its products is exorbitant and its profits are similarly exorbitant.
The automobile companies of Canada, which are almost exclusively U.S. owned, have been very careful not to reveal the profits they make in Canada. Canadian governments have been too stupid to pass legislation that would require the automobile companies, like any other company in Canada, to issue annual statements detailing their turnover, profits, capital investments and so on. Several years ago both the Chrysler Corporation and American Motors did submit figures, not to the Canadian government but to the United States securities and exchange commission at a time when the companies were trying to float a new loan in the United States. These figures indicated that the net profit amounted to 30 per cent on invested capital per year. Although the figures applied to those particular years, that is probably their proportion of profit every year.
The Toronto Globe and Mail, which is not a very radical newspaper but is very widely read and respected in the business community of Canada, had this to say about the profits of automobile manufacturers in a report on January 19, 1965:
According to one estimate, the average annual profit of the auto manufacturers often has run to around 30 per cent of their net worth, that is the total amount of their invested capital, compared with a more normal 10 to 15 per cent return in other industries.
While the balance sheets of most of the major producers are closed to public scrutiny, one federal official estimated that in a good year the profit earned by one of the leading Canadian auto producers might run as high as 80 to 90 per cent of invested capital.
This calculation is made by the writer of this article in the Toronto Globe and Mail and I think it merits the minister's study.

Having made these comments about the prices of Canadian automobiles failing to come down and about what 1 consider to be the exorbitant profits made by the automobile manufacturing companies, I should like to deal for a moment with some of the good things that the minister had to say about the results of the auto pact. I agree with him that there has been a large increase in the production of automobiles in Canada, and this is good. The trade imbalance has been reduced from $683 million in 1966 to $350 million. Those are the figures I understood the minister to give when he spoke earlier and I jotted them down. The average level of employment has increased from about 60,000 workers in this country to 80,000. An increase of 20,000 is substantial and this too is all to the good. Productivity has already increased, as I have said. The minister estimates that the gap in productivity between the United States and Canada has been reduced to 20 per cent.
The minister went on to say that a program of loans has been worked out for automobile parts manufacturers. As I noted his statement, 68 loans to a value of $55 million have been made to automobile parts manufacturers. That is good. We have also been told that automobile manufacturers have been permitted to benefit, to the tune of several million dollars, by tariff arrangements with respect to machinery that is not made in Canada. That also is good. Nevertheless the difficulties with regard to this plan which were discussed in 1965 are still there. Those difficulties were spoken about eloquently last week during the estimates of the Minister of Labour by the hon. members for Essex East and Essex West, who represent the automobile workers of Windsor and who know more about these problems than I do, coming from Winnipeg.

Without going over ground that has previously been gone over, may I commend to the hon. member for Essex East a reading of Hansard for the month of May, 1965. It will be seen by so doing that a number of hon. members, of whom I was one, predicted then to the minister responsible for industry precisely what would happen. We said that although productivity would go up this would prove of little consolation to workers who might be laid off. Right now about 1,000 Ford workers have been laid off.

The minister ought to read the speeches of the hon. member for Essex East who told us precisely what would happen. I say that what has happened ought not to have happened. When the plan was drafted the union representing the Canadian automobile workers did not oppose it. In fact, the union endorsed and welcomed the plan and called on the government to take precautionary steps to ensure that the workers would receive the kind of sweet, loving attention which the government gave to the employers. We looked after the employers in this field by giving them what amounted to a $50 million subsidy under new tariff arrangements.
When the employers are caught in a squeeze because of any rationalization brought about by the automobile plan, they are looked after. Yet, as the union said in 1965, the government simply refuses to make a similar kind of provision for the employees. The government knew what would happen because the unions warned it. The minister need only look at the correspondence that two former ministers of labour, Mr. Nicholson and the present Minister of Manpower and Immigration, have had on the subject to see that this is so. The unions proposed a series of measures to protect workers who would be caught in the squeeze.
Credit must be given where credit is owing, and I must say that the minister was interested in this matter. The deputy minister of labour, Dr. Hawthorne, was most interested in the union's proposals. Why did the government not go ahead with those proposals? I will tell you why, Mr. Chairman. Because the companies refused to co-operate-that's why

-and because the government did not have the courage to bring in legislation implementing the union's proposals and the proposals made by Mr. Justice Freedman.
Although I was not here last week when the estimates of the Department of Labour were before the house I read the minister's speech and I commend him for it. After the speeches we had from the former minister of labour, last week's speech certainly sounded wonderful. All the same, two years have elapsed since Mr. Justice Freedman handed down his report. How long must we wait before the suggestions of the report are implemented in legislation? The former minister did not think it was necessary to pass legislation in this field, believing that the companies, out of the goodness of their hearts, would adopt the basic principles of the Freedman report through collective bargaining. Of course, that has not happened. How many legal or illegal stoppages must we undergo before the government brings in legislation to implement the suggestions of the Freedman report?
Now we are told that we must wait for the Woods commission to make its report. When will that be? If the Woods commission makes no special recommendations about the basic principles of the Freedman report, must we wait for the findings of another committee or another commission? We are dealing with human lives and, at the moment, with 1,000 jobs. The Ford Motor Company at Windsor has acted in a way no different from the way thousands of other Canadian corporate employers have acted.
Our labour legislation says that except where there is a special clause in a labour-management agreement that prohibits a company from acting in a certain manner, a company has the right to manage its own affairs. The corollary to all this is that when a company makes a change such as is now contemplated while an agreement is in force the union by law is precluded from striking. While an agreement between the union and the company is in force the union is estopped from doing anything about the sort of change we see here. I can only say that had the government listened to what the unions said in 1965, had it set up the kind of labour-management discussions that was then suggested and had it followed through with the legislation that was proposed, this kind of thing would not have happened. The government must have known what would happen if it did not listen.

I concur with the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East who said that it is a disgrace in 1968 for the Ford Motor Company, which has tremendous assets, not to give its employees more than a week's notice that they are to be laid off for a year or 18 months. We in the U.A.W. are pleased that an agreement has been worked out by the U.S. and Canadian governments to provide for a common market in automobiles and parts.
We have long favoured trade liberalization and expansion and we have advocated for many years the creation of such a common market.

The auto workers went on to spell out in detail what the government and the industry should do to protect workers from the kind of thing which has been happening during the past month at the Ford plant. Mr. George Burt, at that time the Canadian director of the U.A.W., said in his report to the Canadian U.A.W. council in March of 1965:
Up to this point, to our knowledge, neither the Department of Industry which developed this "free trade" program, nor the Department of Labour which is responsible for the manpower and employment aspects of the program, have made any study whatever of the impact of this program on Canadian workers' jobs and incomes. It is therefore absolutely essential that we should be in a position to inform Mr. Drury and Mr. MacEachen of what is taking place under this program as soon as that information becomes available so that we can demand that action be taken, and if it is not, then those that speak for us in the House of Commons in Ottawa can demand to know of the government why the necessary action has not been taken.
Well, we have been asking this government for two and a half years to take action and, as I have indicated, nothing has been done. When we discussed this matter two and a half years ago the hon. member for Essex West, as he then was, scoffed at these pleas. He said we were making mountains out of molehills and anticipating difficulties which would not arise. I notice that the hon. member made a very different speech last week from the one he made in May, 1965. He has learned that we were right and that the auto workers' union was right in predicting what would happen.
The United Auto Workers' union sent a memorandum to the minister of labour early in 1965 spelling out the six steps which it believed the government should endorse so as to cushion the shock of the kind of dislocation which is now taking place. I should like to put this memorandum on record again in the hope that the government and the present minister will have learned something from experience. Even though the implementation of the proposals at this date would be late in coming, it is better to be late than to be altogether wrong. Here is what was proposed

The specific proposals put forward by Mr. Burt at that time on behalf of the workers in the auto industry look like a charter of human rights. Had the government taken action at that time, the present hardship and dislocation might have been avoided. I submit that the government could have done one of two things. First, it could have used the power it had at that time with the companies. After all, the government could have refused to go ahead with the auto pact, an arrangement which would obviously bring definite advantages to the companies. Alternatively, the government might have passed legislation to protect the rights of the workers. Instead, the government chose to ignore the pleas made on behalf of those employed in the industry, so today we are facing a serious problem at Ford in Windsor. Tomorrow it may arise in Oshawa, as it did several

years ago. Next month or next year it may arise in Oakville, and so on down the line.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
If the government really believes in the just society, about which the Prime Minister has spoken so often and so eloquently, it ought to translate such glib phrases and slogans into concrete action, into legislation, into direction to the automobile companies whereby the benefits of the agreement worked out by the Department of Industry will give the workers the same kind of protection as the government's programs now give to the automobile manufacturers, a group of companies which needs less assistance from the government of Canada than any other group of manufacturers in the country. This agreement has had a very profound effect on the Canadian economy as a whole and some pretty drastic effects on individual automobile workers.
The agreement has been in effect for almost three years. Unless the government is prepared to do as I suggest I can only conclude, and I am sure the 380 workers already laid off at the Ford company and the 700 more who will be laid off during the next few months can only conclude, that the just society was just an election gimmick on the part of the Prime Minister.

Mr. Chairman, we have heard various gloomy words from the other side of the chamber. I would like to emphasize some of the more positive aspects of the Kennedy round tariff reductions which will have a decisive and favourable effect on the Canadian economy. The successful conclusion of these negotiations has provided Canada with new access to world markets for a much wider range of Canadian products than was the case in the past, including many manufactured goods. These new opportunities for increasing the sale of our products abroad have made it possible for Canadian industry to realize some of the economies of volume production and greater specialization which other countries enjoyed in the past. I think these factors will be very important to our country too.
The improved access to export markets is a most important factor in shaping our economy to meet the competitive demands of the future. I think we all know that this is inevitable in a country such as ours which devotes about 20 per cent of its production to exports.
The Kennedy round was the most extensive trade and tariff negotiation ever undertaken
December 2, 1968

Supply-Industry
under the auspices of the GATT. The negotiations covered all classes of products and dealt not only with tariffs but also with non-tariff barriers. To give some idea of the scope of the negotiations, there were more than 50 countries participating in them, including all the major trading countries and some 30 of the so-called developing countries.
The major participating countries are making tariff cuts on 70 per cent of their dutiable industrial imports, of which some two-thirds will be reductions of 50 per cent or more. Under the most favoured nation principle of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade these concessions are automatically and unconditionally being extended to all GATT members.
The most important long term benefits for the Canadian economy are the across the board reductions being made by the principal industrial countries in the manufactured goods sector. The 50 per cent reductions being made for a wide range of goods in this area will result in final rates of 10 per cent or less for a very wide range of manufactured products.
Canada is a relatively small supplier of manufactured goods on the world markets. Therefore we see that already there has been a marked growth in Canadian exports of fully manufactured products in recent years. As a matter of fact exports of such products have risen from 14 per cent to 34 per cent of the total Canadian export trade. To look at this in another way, exports of fully manufactured goods have grown at a rate nearly five times faster than that of total exports.
While the Kennedy round tariff reductions will substantially assist in expanding trade in products now being exported, they will also encourage Canadian producers to look into the possibilities of exporting goods which hitherto may have sold only in domestic markets. This twofold expandion of trade is important for several reasons. While our traditional resource-based industries will remain an important factor in our export trade, the increase in trade in these products would not provide for the amount of expansion required in our over-all trade to sustain our economy at viable levels. Therefore we must concentrate on the manufactured goods sector, which is the fastest growing sector in world trade. Expansion in this sector and in the service industries will have to provide the employment opportunities for our rapidly growing labour force.

I would now like, Mr. Chairman, to make a few brief remarks about the Kennedy round as a whole. Those negotiations are the sixth of the great tariff negotiations which took place under GATT since its interim application in 1947. They were also the most important trade negotiations held until then-if one considers the number of participating countries, the value of the trade operations that will be affected by those agreements and the consequences of the tariff reductions.
The negotiations covered all types of industrial and agricultural products and dealt not only with customs tariffs but also with some non-tariff problems. It was agreed that, as much as possible, and subject to general reciprocity, the tariff negotiations would tend to realize uniform or general linear reductions of 50 per cent.
Obviously, Mr. Chairman, the advantages arising from the tremendous scope of the Kennedy Round have a decisive and lasting effect on Canadian exporters as a whole. As the export trade accounts for-as I just said in English-20 per cent of the total Canadian production, these negociations will have a great impact on the whole economy, provided the Canadian export industry is in a position to avail itself of the opportunities offered in the coming years.
It is in the manufactured goods sector that the tariff reductions are most striking and most important. It is the sector that offers the greatest possibilities for the expansion of the export trade. The adjustment assistance program will be available for a specialization and a restructuration of the Canadian industry which will be essential if manufactured goods are benefit by an easier access to export markets.
Mr. Chairman, may I refer for a few moments to that program. Maybe we have heard too much about what is wrong with the Kennedy Round, and not enough about what we have done here, in Canada, to promote the export of products covered by the Kennedy Round.
Mr. Chairman, the adjustment program comprises three parts.
First, the underwriting by the government of an important part of the risk of loss which the industrial assistance loans granted by private lenders involves; secondly, in exceptional cases, direct loans granted by the government to companies disadvantaged or in danger to be seriously disadvantaged because of the reductions of the Canadian tariff and

If the benefits are much greater in respect of military-oriented industry, research and development, how will we ever encourage serious research and development in the non-military segments of our industry? I should like the minister to deal with this question at some point.
